title: The blue wave is mostly in red states. That's a little weird.
subtitle: Still Counting EP3. Plus some quick thoughts on that NYT poll in Maine.
contentHtml:
We tape Still Counting on Wednesday late mornings, and then shoot to get the episode turned around by Wednesday late afternoon/early evening. When I publish the episodes here at the newsletter, I’ll aim to add more context, but Silver Bulletin work tends to pile up midweek, so that will often take until Thursday morning.

Either way, we sincerely appreciate all the support you’ve shown for the show, and reviews, comments, likes and subscribes remain very much appreciated.

The context: Polling has been great for Democrats. But is it too good to be true?

A New York Times/Portland Press Herald/Siena poll out this morning had some disappointing news for Democrats, with Susan Collins leading Troy Jackson by 3 points in Maine.

Other NYT polls had Democrats ahead by 5 points in Michigan and New Hampshire. Still, this poll feels like a “heat check” for Democrats. Since Labor Day, Democrats have been zooming ahead in FLIPR along with pretty much every model or polling average or prediction market that you might want to look at. At times, it’s literally been hard to find contrary data points to the hypothesis of a huge D sweep. So the poll serves as a reminder that picking up four Senate seats is never easy.

The NYT is a very honest (and highly-rated) pollster that doesn’t herd. So a variety of interpretations are possible:

  1. Noise/sampling error;

  2. Collins being particularly tough to beat;

  3. Democrats’ polling strength being concentrated in red states, not blue states.

The third interpretation is the one I want to briefly explore here.

For full access to FLIPR and the rest of Silver Bulletin’s midterms coverage, please consider becoming a subscriber.

As Galen, Clare and I discussed, there’s a pretty obvious bull case for Democrats. Polls have shown Democrats massively overperforming in red states, especially in the Midwest. And there’s a coherent story behind that:

  • The groups that swung most toward Trump since 2016 — namely white working-class voters and Hispanics — are finally souring on him, as you might expect for a president with a -23 net approval rating. Trump’s approval ratings weren’t great in 2018, but they were better than this: a mere -12 at this point in the election cycle. And that was a good midterm for Democrats anyway. So maybe now the bottom is falling out, and exactly those areas where Trump has made the biggest gains since 2016 are now the most vulnerable for Republicans.

  • In the heartland, this is exacerbated by extremely high gas and diesel prices, putting some surprising states like Iowa and Kansas in play.

  • And maybe there’s a bit of a throw-the-bums out mentality. As we’ve observed, being the incumbent party — which Republicans are in most of the key races — has been as much of a disadvantage as an advantage in recent elections.

By contrast, though, Democrats’ polling has been pretty “mid” in blue states.

Sure, maybe Collins, as one of the few truly moderate members left in Congress, is an exception to the throw-the-bums out mood. The other NYT polls were perfectly fine for Democrats. In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed had led by 3.3 points in the FLIPR polling average prior to the NYT poll, so the poll should actually help him. The poll is consistent with El-Sayed paying a progressive “tax” of a few points, but probably still winning.

In some ways, it’s more surprising to see Chris Pappas only ahead by 5 points in New Hampshire — or Peggy Flanagan in a close-ish race in Minnesota, or Kathy Hochul struggling to achieve a double-digit lead in New York. (Though other polls disagree there.)

So if you take the polls at face value, we’re seeing a blue wave that’s … overwhelmingly concentrated in red states. As I wrote, there’s a coherent story behind it. And the evidence for it has been consistent enough that it probably has to count as the “base case”.

But there’s also some risk here for Democrats. Precisely those groups with whom they’re making the largest gains are those where polls have most overestimated Democrats in recent years.

There are also potentially huge, lopsided rewards. If the map is reverting more to something pre-Trump-like, that was a map where Barack Obama won Iowa and Ohio twice. Meanwhile, in the House, Republican gerrymanders in states like Florida and Texas were implicitly premised on the GOP having made permanent gains among Hispanics. If those are even partly undone, the Florida map in particular could turn into a dummymander. Our Lite (“polls only”) forecast for the House is probably the best way to envision this — look at that big, asymmetric right tail for Democrats. Those are basically 1994-style maps in reverse in which Democrats break through to districts where they had no business competing.

But this is potentially a somewhat boom-or-bust story for Democrats. The bear/bust case is probably less about them losing Minnesota or New Hampshire than about those gains in red states being a mirage.

I’m sure we’ll write about this more in the coming weeks.

Silver Bulletin news and notes

  • I mentioned that midweeks are busy. That’s partly because we’ve traditionally updated our NFL products, ELWAY and QBERT, on Wednesdays. Like FLIPR, ELWAY is a very “data-hungry” model, and wrangling all that data is a chore. AI tools help with exactly this kind of thing, so we’re hoping to get to the point where the turnaround is faster: perhaps one update Tuesday/Wednesday and then another on Friday or Saturday with the results of the Thursday Night game + injury updates. It might take a couple of weeks to get there, and we don’t want to pinky-swear promise anything until after the midterms are over. Automating things almost always helps in the long-run, but it can take more time in the short term. We’ve also toned down ELWAY’s injury adjustments, as we think those may have been picking up on some residual context that didn’t pertain to injuries themselves. (Teams that have a lot of injuries often also have a lot of other things that are going wrong.)

  • Eli wrote yesterday about whether the ostensible Republican fundraising advantage is as meaningful as headlines sometimes imply that it is.

  • And I wrote about the effect of diesel prices on the map.

  • I also wrote about why expert ratings are so much less bullish for Democrats than polls, models and prediction markets. The Maine poll is a valid reason for concern for Democrats. I’m not sure that the expert ratings are.
